one_liner: Go msgpack2 code generator with versioned, typed field names; ~15% faster writes than gogo/protobuf in author's 2017 benchmark.
what_it_does: greenpack is a go generate code generator plus runtime package, forked from tinylib/msgp. It emits MarshalMsg/UnmarshalMsg methods (for []byte) and EncodeMsg/DecodeMsg methods (for msgp.Writer/Reader streams) for Go structs. The output is ordinary msgpack2 maps whose keys are the field name plus a zid version number and a type clue (e.g. "Name_zid00_str"). Any msgpack library can read it, and Go readers get field versioning and exact integer types back. It is not a protobuf drop-in: there is no .proto IDL, the wire format is different, and the Go struct with `zid` tags is the schema.
how_it_is_fast: It uses reflection-free code generation inherited from tinylib/msgp. Marshal pre-sizes the output with the generated Msgsize() via msgp.Require, then writes each field key as a precomputed msgpack byte literal (`o = append(o, 0xae, 0x4e, ...)`) followed by a type-specific Append* call into a caller-supplied []byte. Repeated marshals into a reused buffer therefore allocate nothing. Unmarshal reads map keys zero-copy and dispatches through a compiled Go string switch to per-field decoders, mutates existing slices and maps in place, and zeroes missing fields by replaying a msgpack nil through the same switch (a fixed-size NilBitsStack) instead of allocating.
when_to_use: Go services whose structs must be readable from Python, R or JS with a stock msgpack library and no generated code or schema file.
You want the Go struct definition to be the schema: no .proto/IDL, no protoc or C++ toolchain, just `//go:generate greenpack`.
Write-heavy paths that can reuse an output buffer: MarshalMsg(buf) appends into the caller's slice. The 2017 run measured 129 ns/op and 0 allocs/op for a 6-field struct.
Schemas that evolve over time: numbered zid fields, `deprecated` tombstones and conflict detection at generate time, plus signed/unsigned integer types that stock msgpack encoders lose.
Pipelines that need serialization hooks (PreSave/PostLoad, e.g. to flatten trees) or generated MariaDB read/write methods (`-sql mariadb`).
when_not_to_use: Wire size matters. Every key carries the field name, zid and type clue, so the benchmark struct encoded to ~142 bytes, against ~59 for ZebraPack (derived from the MB/s and ns/op columns). Use ZebraPack, `-omit-clue`/`-alltuple`, or protobuf instead.
You need C++ or other non-Go code generation. None exists; the author points C++ users to generic msgpack libraries (issue #16).

You are choosing it for faster reads than gogo/protobuf. The only published greenpack read number actually measured ZebraPack, and the author's 2024 CBOR comparison shows greenpack Unmarshal at 322 ns/op with 2 allocs/op.

Code that relies on generics or shared pointers. Type-parameterized fields are skipped unless you pass `-generics=true`, which the author says is much slower. Automatic pointer dedup has been off by default since v0.529.0 because of unresolved errors, and Marshal/Unmarshal never supported it.
You need a large-team maintenance guarantee. It is a single-author project; a report that map[int64]map[int8]T writes no data (#12) was closed without a fix.

integration.dependencies: runtime package github.com/glycerine/greenpack/msgp (depends on glycerine/fwd, 4d63.com/tz); the generator also uses golang.org/x/tools and shurcooL/go-goon; goconvey for tests
integration.platforms: any Go target; pure Go, uses unsafe string/slice casts (an appengine build tag provides a no-unsafe variant)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. From the source, generated Marshal/Unmarshal keep decode state (NilBitsStack) in locals, while msgp.Writer/Reader are per-stream objects that hold dedup state.

gotchas: `-fast-strings` makes decoded strings alias the input buffer through unsafe, so that buffer must not be reused. In current master, msgp/read_bytes.go ReadStringBytes takes the zero-copy path only when `err != nil`, so successful reads still copy with string(v). Measure allocations yourself before relying on the zero-alloc claim.

Cross-language readers see extras. time.Time is msgpack extension type 5 (normalized to UTC), not the standard -1 timestamp, and time.Duration is extension 7. EncodeMsg streams also add an "@" struct-name key unless you pass `-no-structnames-onwire`; the MarshalMsg path does not.

All fields are omitempty by default, so zero values never reach the wire and absent keys decode as zero. The nil-replay stack that implements this is fixed at 8 nested struct levels (MaxNestedStructPointerDepth) and panics beyond that.
Go module versioning: tags were renamed to v0.xxx.0, and the proxy still reports the old non-module v5.1.2 as @latest. Pin an explicit v0.5xx.0 tag (tags go up to v0.541.0).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick greenpack over ZebraPack (same author: 120 vs 129 ns/op writes, ~59 vs ~142-byte payload) when other-language consumers must decode with any msgpack library and no schema, because greenpack data is fully self-describing. Pick ZebraPack or Karmem when raw Go speed or wire size matters more, and SBE, Bebop or Apache Fory (C++) for C++-side work, since greenpack has no C++ generator.
verified_claims_summary: In the author's 2017 fork of alecthomas/go_serialization_benchmarks (6-field struct, 3.1 GHz Core i7 MacBook Pro 13", Go version unconfirmed; the header says 1.8beta2), GreenPackMarshal took 129 ns/op with 0 allocs, against 152 ns/op with 1 alloc (64 B) for gogo/protobuf's proto.Marshal. greenpack wrote into a reused 512-byte buffer while gogo allocated its output on every call. The 224 vs 240 ns/op read row is invalid because BenchmarkGreenPackUnmarshal calls ZebraPack's ZMarshalMsg/ZUnmarshalMsg.
status_note: Actively maintained by its single author (last commit 2026-01-23, tags up to v0.541.0). MIT-licensed, pure Go, and used via go generate, so it is easy to adopt in Go projects.
